blocks.text: Accordingly Diodorus, book 1, where he speaks of the island of Meroe: Πρὸς δὲ τούτοις (λέγουσιν) ἔχειν πλῆθος ἐβένου [Pros de toutois (legousin) echein plēthos ebenou], Moreover they say that it has an abundance of ebony. And Pliny records that the rare tree ebony was brought to Nero (fetched) from as far as Meroe, a distance of 996 miles from Syene, the boundary of the empire. But in these words of Servius too, And yet it grows also in Egypt, there is an obvious error. For he had certainly written, And yet it grows also in Ethiopia, as what follows shows: But by India we understand the whole region of Ethiopia. This would be ἀνακόλουθα [anakoloutha] if we read in Egypt. For Servius says this on the passage of Virgil discussed above,

which he maintains is true, even though ebony also grows in Ethiopia, because the name of India includes Ethiopia. But if you say that ebony grows in Egypt, this excuse will not hold. For Egypt is one thing, Ethiopia another; nor is there anyone who understands Egypt by the name of India. Fifth, ebony and ivory, together with gold, were the constant tribute of the Ethiopians. Hence in Diodorus, book 1, p. 35, when Sesoosis (var. Sesostres), the most ancient king of the Egyptians, had subdued the Ethiopians, ἠνάγκασε τὸ ἔθνος φόρους τελεῖν, ἔβενον, καὶ χρυσὸν, καὶ τῶν ἐλεφάντων τοὺς ὀδόντας [ēnankase to ethnos phorous telein, ebenon, kai chryson, kai tōn elephantōn tous odontas], he imposed on the nation as tribute ebony, and gold, and elephants' teeth. The Persians are read to have exacted the same things from the same Ethiopians. Herodotus, Muse 3, ch. 97: Ἀγινέουσι δὲ καὶ τὸ μέχρι ἐμεῦ δύο χοίνικας ἀπύρου χρυσίου, καὶ διηκοσίας φαλάγγας ἐβένου, καὶ ἐλέφαντος ὀδόντας μεγάλους εἴκοσι· [Agineousi de kai to mechri emeu dyo choinikas apyrou chrysiou, kai diēkosias phalangas ebenou, kai elephantos odontas megalous eikosi] Down to my own time (the Ethiopians, as a triennial tribute to the Persians) bring two choenixes of apyrous gold (that is, not yet tried by fire), and two hundred logs of ebony, and twenty large elephant tusks. For the region is rich in these three things, as the same author writes in ch. 114: Αὕτη δὲ χρυσόν τε φέρει πολλὸν, καὶ ἐλέφαντας ἀμφιλαφέας, καὶ δένδρεα πάντα ἄγρια, καὶ ἔβενον· [Hautē de chryson te pherei pollon, kai elephantas amphilapheas, kai dendrea panta agria, kai ebenon] This land produces much gold, and very large elephants, and wild trees of every kind, and ebony. Pliny too, book [II, 717] 12, ch. 4, where he states of ebony that by way of tribute the Ethiopians paid to the kings of Persia every third year a hundred logs of its wood, together with gold and ivory. And in the procession of Ptolemy Philadelphus, according to Callixenus of Rhodes, Ethiopians are reported to have carried these same things. [col. 142] Ἐχόμενοι τούτων ἦσαν (he says) Αἰθίοπες δωροφόροι, ὧν οἱ μὲν ἔφερον ὀδόντας ἑξακοσίους, ἕτεροι δὲ ἐβένου κορμοὺς δισχιλίους, ἄλλοι χρυσοῦ καὶ ἀργυρίου κρατῆρας ἑξήκοντα, καὶ ψήγματα χρυσίου [Echomenoi toutōn ēsan … Aithiopes dōrophoroi, hōn hoi men epheron odontas hexakosious, heteroi de ebenou kormous dischilious, alloi chrysou kai argyriou kratēras hexēkonta, kai psēgmata chrysiou]. Next to these came Ethiopians bearing gifts, some of whom carried six hundred (elephants') tusks, others two thousand logs of ebony, others sixty bowls of gold and silver, and gold dust. Accordingly, at the festival of Adonis celebrated with great pomp at Alexandria under the same king, the Syracusan women, on seeing the ebony and the gold and the abundant ivory, burst out in these words, Idyll 15, line 123:
Ὦ ἔβενος, ὢ χρυσὸς, ὢ ἐκ λευκῶ ἐλέφαντος Αἰετώ! [Ō ebenos, ō chrysos, ō ek leukō elephantos Aietō!]
